description: Dark green plates shut around a yellow-green star, and the moss on them is still growing. It cuts and it mends.
lore: Set one on a shelf and leave it a year and the moss will have got further. Not much further — a plate's width up the shaded side — but further, on a stone that is fed nothing, watered by nothing and kept indoors. Of everything that comes back in a bag off a broken shape, this is the only piece still doing something, and the people who handle stones by the sackful stopped finding that remarkable a long time ago and still, as a rule, keep this one where they can see it.

They grade it by the star. Hold it up against a fire and the light comes through the seams between the plates; on a good one the yellow-green runs out along every crack to the rim, so the whole egg is drawn on in lines, and on a poor one it has stayed down in the middle and shows from a single angle. That is not a judgement about looks. A stone whose star reaches the rim closes a cut while you are still swinging. One that does not will get round to it.

It is also the one stone people argue about where to put. The convention is to set a hard piece against an edge, and against an edge this one behaves exactly as the trade expects of it. But the mending only runs while the stone is near the body, and there are fitters who will tell you flatly that a blade wastes it — put it in the breastplate, wear it against the ribs, and it works on you all day whether or not there is anything in front of you. The counter is that a stone spending its afternoon mending a man who has not been touched is a stone doing very little. Both sides are describing one fact and neither will say it plainly, so here it is: growth does not distinguish. It goes into whatever it is set against. Turn it on a shape and it opens it; hold it to yourself and it closes you. It is not doing two things.

There is a heap at the edge of every field in every country, which is why this is the one good stone a working person can expect to own, and why the other thing about it can be tested. Take twenty of them off twenty broken heaps, a century and a border apart, and lay them out on a cloth. You cannot sort them. The plating runs the same way, the star sits at the same depth, the moss is the same moss. A stone out of something that once fell is always an individual — a facet rubbed smooth by whatever it did ten thousand times, a flaw you would know again in the dark. These have no such thing, because there was never anyone in one of them to differ. It is the same fact that makes a gold coin a gold coin, arriving from a direction that pleases very few people.
